Dear Administrator Oz: 
 
Lundbeck Pharmaceuticals LLC (Lundbeck) is writing to comment on the proposed rule 
concerning Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs, issued by the 
Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) on April 14, 2026.1 
Lundbeck is a global biopharmaceutical company focusing exclusively on brain health.  With 
more than 70 years of experience in neuroscience, we are committed to improving the lives 
of people with neurological and psychiatric diseases.  As a focused innovator, we strive for 
our research and development programs to tackle some of the most complex neurological 
challenges.  We develop transformative medicines targeting diseases for which there are 
few or no treatments available, expanding into neuro-specialty and neuro-rare diseases 
from our strong legacy within psychiatry and neurology.  Lundbeck reinvests 20 to 25% of 
 
1 91 Fed. Reg. 19890 (Apr. 14, 2026). 
2 
 
global revenue in R&D and has 172 active clinical trial sites in the United States.  With US 
headquarters in Deerfield, Illinois, we employ over 1,000 people in the US and operate a US 
Drug Discovery Hub in La Jolla, California and biologics manufacturing facility in Bothell, 
Washington. 
Lundbeck appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Interoperability and Prior 
Authorization proposed rule.  Under this proposed rule, CMS aims to improve the electronic 
exchange of health care data by increasing interoperability across the health care industry, 
with a particular focus on streamlining prior authorization processes for drugs across a set 
of “impacted payers”: Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and qualified health plans 
(QHPs) on federally-facilitated exchanges and Small Business Health Options Program (FF-
SHOP). CMS would require these impacted payers to make electronic prior authorization 
available for drugs and to extend existing interoperability requirements — previously 
applicable to non-drug items and services — to drug prior authorizations, reducing 
administrative burden on patients and providers.  
We appreciate that through this proposed rule, CMS is responding to the many commenters 
urging it to extend the prior authorization streamlining measures in its 2024 Interoperability 
and Prior Authorization rule2 to drugs.  Imposing timelines for prior authorization decisions 
will be an especially critical improvement to the prior authorization process for prescription 
drugs.   
Lundbeck also applauds CMS’ ongoing leadership in enabling electronic communications 
pathways between patients, providers, and payers. The foundation for many reforms is built 
on more rapid communication between these parties with the potential to streamline 
patients’ access to medications recommended by their providers.  As CMS knows, troubling 
recent reports documenting the burdens of prior authorization requests on providers and the 
risks for patients --- including treatment delays and abandonment – call urgently for reforms 
in this area.3  Lundbeck is hopeful that the prior authorization improvements and 
accountability measures in this proposed rule will enable providers to dedicate more time to 
patient care and ultimately improve patients’ health.

2025), https://www.ajmc.com/view/ama-survey-highlights-growing-burden-of-prior-authorization-on-physicians-patients 
(discussing the burdens of prior authorization on providers).  
3 
 
Lundbeck fully supports and incorporates by reference the comments submitted by our 
trade association, the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA).  
We write separately to emphasize a few key points that can enhance the final rule’s impact 
on patient outcomes.  
Our comments can be summarized as follows: 
• CMS should require all impacted payers addressed in the proposed rule to respond 
to prior authorization requests for drugs within 24 hours. 
• To help ensure the success of prior authorization reform, CMS should build in 
accountability measures for impacted payers. In particular, if a payer fails to meet a 
prior authorization response deadline, that failure should be treated as an approval 
of the prior authorization request – thus providing coverage with no further delays – 
or at the very least should be treated as a denial that is immediately appealable. 
• CMS’ proposal to require a specific reason for denial of a prior authorization request 
has significant potential to reduce treatment delays and should be fleshed out in a 
way that maximizes its effectiveness. CMS should provide impacted payers with a 
standardized list of denial reasons to choose from and a free text space in which 
payers should provide any additional information that will give the provider a better, 
more actionable understanding of immediate next steps. 
• CMS should use the publicly reported prior authorization metrics as an oversight 
tool, including monitoring whether imposing shorter deadlines for prior authorization 
decisions for drugs has any unintended consequences such as increased denials or 
(where relevant) extensions. 
• CMS should carefully evaluate all of the recommendations for reform it receives in 
response to the step therapy RFI and, in particular, should consider near-term 
adoption of the following steps: 
o CMS should mandate that payers use readily available electronic tools such 
as payer APIs to obtain all the information they can about a patient’s clinical 
history from other payers, and use that information to determine if the patient 
has already met some or all of the steps in the payer’s step therapy protocol. 
o Given the burdens to providers and the risks to patients associated with prior 
authorization and step therapy, CMS should limit the frequency of such 
utilization management barriers. Specifically, once a patient has undergone a 
step therapy protocol and receives authorization to take the drug that is their

prescriber’s first choice, the authorization should last for at least a year and 
should not lapse due to any changes in the prescribed dosage for the drug.  
I. 
CMS Should Consider the Feasibility of Imposing a Uniform 24-Hour Deadline 
to Respond to Prior Authorization Requests for Drugs 
CMS proposes the following deadlines for decisions on prior authorization requests:  72 
hours for standard requests and 24 hours for expedited requests for QHP issuers on the 
FFEs; 24 hours for Medicaid fee-for-service (FFS) programs and managed care plans 
(except for certain drugs bundled with other items and services that have longer deadlines); 
and 24 hours for CHIP FFS programs and managed care entities.4 
With respect to Medicare Advantage (MA), CMS explains that under current regulations,  
MA organizations must notify the enrollee (and the prescribing 
physician or other prescriber involved, as appropriate) of a 
determination regarding coverage of a Part B drug as 
expeditiously as the enrollee’s health condition requires, but no 
later than 72 hours after receiving the standard request and no 
later than 24 hours after receiving the expedited request.  
Similarly, Part D sponsors, including MA–PDs, have the same 
requirements for prior authorization decisions on Part D drugs 
(with the possibility of an extension).5 
CMS states that “[g]iven the existing prior authorization decision timeframe requirements for 
Part B and Part D drugs, we do not believe that additional proposals for MA organizations or 
Part D sponsors are necessary or appropriate at this time.”6  
CMS’ basic proposal to establish timely deadlines for drug prior authorization decisions for 
all impacted payers is an important initiative that we strongly support.  At the same time, we 
have concerns about adoption of differing deadlines across payers and believe a uniform 
approach would have key benefits for providers and patients and most effectively advance 
CMS’ goals.  Thus, we urge CMS to consider the feasibility of adopting a uniform 24-hour 
 
4 91 Fed. Reg. at 20039-40. 
5 91 Fed. Reg. at 19935; see also 42 CFR 422.568(b)(3) and 42 CFR 422.572(a)(2). 
6 91 Fed. Reg. at 19935. 
5 
 
deadline for drug prior authorization decisions across the full set of impacted payers 
addressed in this rulemaking. 
By imposing a uniform 24-hour rule for drug prior authorization decisions, CMS could 
shorten the timeline for certain payers to make prior authorization decisions that can take 
weeks today, thereby accelerating patient access to critical drugs.  A uniform 24-hour rule 
across impacted payers will also help providers to anticipate when they can expect 
decisions on prior authorization requests, to understand when they need to highlight the 
urgency of a prior authorization request, to set patients’ expectations, and to respond to 
documentation requests without delay.   
Absent these reforms, patients experience delayed access to needed medications and 
increased health care resource utilization. For commercially insured patients with migraine, 
one in five experienced at least two payer denials due to prior authorization or other 
utilization management.7 This subset of patients had significantly higher rates of ED and 
inpatient encounters for both migraine-related and all-cause reasons within a three-year 
study window.  
Similarly, patients with pediatric epilepsy often (38.4%) encounter prior authorization 
barriers to receiving anti-seizure medications in commercial and Medicaid plans. Less than 
half of these patients received the originally prescribed medicine within seven days. 
Through surveys of parents and caregivers, researchers documented 24 cases of lapsed 
medication, 11 missed doses, seven patients with increased seizures, and one 
hospitalization for status epilepticus (n=164 patients, with 64 encountering prior 
authorization and 32 experiencing at least seven-day delay in receiving medication).8 
It is also critically important to enable physicians and other health care providers and their 
staff to devote more time to patient care and less time to understanding and following prior 
authorization procedures that vary by payer.  The ability to return time to patient care would 
be a key benefit of greater uniformity in these procedures.  CMS has recognized this point, 
stating recently that “[m]ulti-payer alignment [which can involve payers following the same 
policies] makes it easier for providers to deliver value-based care by reducing administrative 
burden and allowing providers to spend more time delivering care to patients.”9 Likewise,

the proposed rule itself states that “The proposals in this proposed rule to extend our extend 
our technical and process requirements for prior authorization to all drugs should improve 
patients’ access to services.  We intend these proposals to create more unified processes 
for providers to request and receive prior authorization for drugs. Such standardization and 
consistency should allow providers to spend more time on patient care and less time on 
administrative tasks and paperwork.”10    
Furthermore, our understanding is that the statutory provisions that give CMS authority to 
impose prior authorization deadlines are broad enough to allow CMS to mandate a 24-hour 
uniform deadline.11 The provision that CMS cites as authority for implementing a prior 
authorization decision deadline for QHP issuers on the FFEs12 states:

certify a health plan as a qualified health plan if—  
(A) such health plan meets the requirements for certification as 
promulgated by the Secretary under subsection (c)(1); and

plan through such Exchange is in the interests of qualified

which such Exchange operates, except that the Exchange may 
not exclude a health plan— (i) on the basis that such plan is a 
fee-for-service plan; (ii) through the imposition of premium price 
controls; or (iii) on the basis that the plan provides treatments 
necessary to prevent patients’ deaths in circumstances the 
Exchange determines are inappropriate or too costly.13 
CMS proposes to impose a prior authorization decision timeline for QHP issuers on the 
FFEs by amending the QHP certification standard it previously finalized, and this language 
in no way limits CMS’ ability to develop a certification standard that requires QHP issuers on 
the FFEs to respond to prior authorization requests within 24 hours.

For MA plans, CMS has the requisite authority to impose a 24-hour decision timeline under 
section 1852 of the Social Security Act (SSA), governing the procedural requirements

Finally, although a 24-hour uniform decision deadline for drug prior authorization decisions 
would expedite the deadline in some cases, payers are able to meet these deadlines 
because of CMS’ investments in interoperability, current proposals to enable electronic 
communication between providers and payers, and real-time provider access to payers’ 
prior authorization policies and documentation requirements. These functionalities will 
increase the feasibility of a 24-hour decision-making timeframe for all impacted payers.  As 
CMS notes in connection with shortening the drug deadline for QHPs,  
We expect that the proposed timeframes … would be feasible  … given the 
notification functionality of the Prior authorization API and NCPDP standards that we 
are proposing QHP issuers on the FFEs to support for electronic prior authorization.  
Those standards support direct electronic communications between payers providers 
about prior authorizations. …[T]hat available technology can accelerate the decision-
making itself ….15 
II. 
CMS Should Ensure Accountability for Meeting Prior Authorization Deadlines 
CMS should pair its proposed deadlines for drug prior authorization decisions with 
accountability measures that incentivize compliance with these timeframes – a critical 
complement to the new deadlines, which as proposed are not backed up by consequences 
for non-compliance.  To address this gap, CMS should specify in the final rule that any 
impacted payer’s failure to meet any prior authorization decision deadline would 
automatically be considered a favorable decision on the request.  We believe this would be 
the most appropriate and effective incentive for compliance with these important deadlines 
because non-compliance otherwise jeopardizes patients’ timely access to medication. 
 
14 Section 1857(e)(1) of the Act also provides that the contract shall contain such other terms or conditions not inconsistent with 
Part C that the Secretary may find necessary and appropriate.                                                                                                                                           
15 91 Fed. Reg. at 19936. 
8 
 
States have widely adopted policies, such as step therapy exception protocols, that provide 
deemed approval if insurers do not act within specified timeframes.16 
Should CMS determine that this approach is not feasible at this time, however, at a 
minimum CMS should adopt the approach reflected in the existing MA regulations. Under 
these regulations, an MA organization’s failure to meet the deadline for the standard or 
expedited prior authorization determination is considered an adverse determination and 
may be appealed.17  CMS could similarly treat a failure to meet any prior authorization 
decision deadline as an adverse determination that is immediately appealable across the 
full set of impacted payers, if it questions the feasibility of treating a failure to meet an 
applicable deadline as an affirmative grant of prior authorization, which is the preferable 
approach most aligned with patient access.  Imposing meaningful accountability on payers 
for failing to meet a prior authorization decision deadline is necessary to spur compliance.18   
As noted above, it is important for all impacted payers to make the best use of the electronic 
prior authorization tools CMS proposes to require to support drug prior authorization 
requests,19 so they can obtain the information they need to make prompt decisions and 
reliably meet these deadlines.  Accountability for noncompliance is essential to ensure that 
impacted payers use available tools to the fullest extent possible to meet the deadlines, 
including carrying out educational and outreach activities to make sure providers 
understand how to submit prior authorization requests in a manner that enables a fast 
turnaround.  Equally essential is strong CMS oversight of payers’ performance to make sure 
they are not responding to the new decision deadlines with increased denials or requests for 
additional information, as discussed further below in Section IV.  
III. 
CMS Should Ensure Payers Effectively Communicate the Reason for a Prior 
Authorization Denial 
CMS proposes that, beginning October 1, 2027, “state Medicaid and CHIP FFS programs, 
Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and QHP issuers on the FFEs 
be required to provide a specific reason to providers when denying a prior authorization

17 42 CFR 422.568(f) and 42 CFR 422.572(f). 
18 In cases where an extension applies, the consequence for failing to provide a decision would not be imposed until the 
extended timeline runs out.

request for drugs.”20  In addition, CMS currently requires MA organizations and Part D plans 
to provide a reason when denying a prior authorization request for a Part B or Part D drug.21 
We appreciate CMS’ proposal to require payers to provide a specific reason to providers 
when denying a prior authorization request for a drug.  Requiring payers to provide a 
specific, actionable reason for denying a prior authorization request is a crucial reform that 
will help providers know what additional information may be useful in appealing a denial and 
more generally will help providers in determining the post-denial steps that would best 
protect the patient’s health. CMS aptly describes the importance of this requirement to 
patient care:  
[B]etter communication between payers and providers could mitigate confusion 
about the status of a prior authorization and why a request was denied. Although 
prior authorization has a role in the health care system, denying services that do not 
meet the payer’s internal coverage or utilization criteria or do not meet regulatory or 
statutory requirements should not adversely impact the health or wellbeing of the 
patient. If a denial is ineffectively communicated, then it could cause a patient to 
delay or abandon treatment….  
… If prior authorization is denied because of a payer’s formulary or utilization 
management policies and that is not clearly communicated, then the provider cannot 
effectively act on behalf of the patient. When a payer provides a specific reason for a 
denial, a provider can take appropriate actions such as resubmitting the request with 
updated information, appealing the decision, or identifying alternative drugs or 
treatments. Payers send denials through various channels—electronically, by mail, 
via portal, or by fax. When doing so, they often use proprietary codes or narrative 
text to communicate the reasons for denial. For some payers, the process of 
communicating denials remains both inefficient and inconsistent. The result is that 
providers may not have timely, clear direction on the next steps for providing 
appropriate care for their patients after a denied prior authorization request.22

Given the stakes for patient outcomes, we recommend that CMS specifically provide payers 
with a drop-down list of standardized denial reasons to choose from and a free text space in 
which they should provide any additional information that explains potential next steps.  A 
standardized list of reasons for denial will promote CMS oversight, by facilitating 
aggregation and evaluation of denial data, and a free text space would be used to prompt 
payers to furnish any additional information that would help the provider understand the 
basis for the denial and respond most effectively, such as specifying exactly what 
information is missing from the original submission.  
This information can reduce ambiguities and confusion and reduce the difficulties and 
delays often associated with getting the patient the most appropriate treatment. As CMS 
notes, it is important to give providers the information they need to make a decision in the 
best interest of their patients: submit additional information, prescribe another drug, or 
appeal the denial.  In our experience at Lundbeck, providers sometimes receive a prior 
authorization decision that omits basic information about what information is needed to 
reverse a denial, even though it may be something as simple as the physician signing a 
form that was submitted unsigned or including the patient’s date of birth.  Therefore, we 
urge CMS to stress the importance of payers providing specific, actionable information in 
their denial decisions that facilitates prompt resolution.   
CMS also could consider developing a standard reason for denial form that payers could 
use (or would be required to use).  For example, CMS could build on the MA Notice of 
Denial of Medical Coverage form mentioned in the proposed rule.23  This form includes the 
following prompt: 
Why was coverage {Insert appropriate term: denied, 
partially approved, stopped, reduced, suspended}?  
We {Insert appropriate term: denied, partially approved, 
stopped, reduced, suspended} the {payment of} {medical 
services/items or Medicare Part B drug or Medicaid drug} listed 
above because {Provide specific rationale for decision and 
include State or Federal law and/or Evidence of Coverage 
provisions to support decision}[.]24

CMS could require payers to answer a similar prompt.  However, we recommend that CMS 
build on this prompt by providing a list of specific, standardized denial reasons impacted 
payers could select and adding language at the end of the prompt that would ask payers to 
include any additional information that would help providers to understand the denial and 
evaluate the available options to respond to the denial. 
IV. 
CMS Should Use Metrics to Oversee Prior Authorization Decisions 
CMS “propos[es] to require impacted payers to annually report certain metrics about prior 
authorizations for all drugs (excluding covered Part D drugs for MA–PDs) by posting this 
information on their public website.”25  Lundbeck strongly supports this proposal, which we 
believe will advance transparency – on issues where currently granular data is rarely 
available, but much needed – and will benefit all of the stakeholders involved in healthcare 
decision-making, research, or policymaking.  These metrics will be helpful to patients in 
making plan enrollment decisions; to providers in selecting payer networks and in evaluating 
the options available to their patients; to payers, in assessing how to improve their 
performance on prior authorization and interoperability requirements; to researchers; and to 
CMS itself as well as other policymakers.  As CMS notes, “publicly reported prior 
authorization metrics for drugs could enable CMS to assess the implementation of the 
policies proposed in this rule” and “help CMS understand the impact of the proposed 
requirements.”26  
Thus, we urge CMS to use these metrics as an oversight tool.  Among other things, CMS 
should use these metrics to monitor whether imposing new deadlines for prior authorization 
decisions has any unintended consequences (such as driving denials or requests for 
extensions through increased documentation requests).  For reasons discussed above, we 
think a uniform 24-hour deadline is reasonable and realistic for the full set of impacted 
payors given the enhanced functionalities payers will have and the capability for accelerated 
communications and data exchanges with providers.  Accordingly, we do not think this 
deadline should require payers to issue denials (or extensions, where available) – but it is 
essential that CMS track the data available to assess this issue and alert payers that it is 
monitoring trends and outliers.  CMS also should generally monitor to see if there is an

26 91 Fed. Reg. at 19949.

uptick in denials, in appeals, and in rates of overturned decisions (which would suggest that 
the original decision to deny prior authorization was not appropriate). 
The proposed rule lays out a set of important reporting metrics that are central to 
understanding payers’ prior authorization practices, the effects of prior authorization on 
patient care, and the effectiveness of CMS policies designed to streamline prior 
authorization and free providers to focus on their patient care mission.  We encourage CMS 
to consider requiring reporting at more granular levels and with metrics broken down by 
drug groups (therapeutic areas, generics vs. brand) where variation in payers’ prior 
authorization practices may be expected but where aggregated reporting may mask access 
challenges. Over time, we urge CMS to publish reports that synthesize the learnings from 
these metrics for the benefit of patients and all healthcare system participants, researchers, 
and policymakers and consider these findings in future rulemaking. 
V. 
Lundbeck Urges CMS to Make Several Modest But Important Step Therapy 
Reforms 
CMS states in the proposed rule that it “is interested in how technology and data sharing, 
such as via the Payer-to-Payer application programming interface (API), might streamline 
the step therapy process by giving payers access to historical drug therapies that a patient 
may have already tried and automating the utilization management process rather than 
requiring providers to submit historical records or attest to prior drug regimens.” The agency 
seeks comment on “how technology may facilitate step therapy determinations and improve 
current step therapy processes.”27 
In response to CMS’ request for comments on how technology might streamline the step 
therapy process, we recommend that CMS mandate that payers use these electronic tools 
to obtain all the information they can about a patient’s clinical history from other payers 
(whether previous or concurrent payers), and use that information to determine if a patient 
has already met some or all of the steps in the payer’s step therapy protocols and whether 
any drugs required under a step therapy protocol would be contraindicated for the patient.   
CMS has invested considerable resources in promoting interoperability, with payers now 
having ready access to troves of information that can inform their step therapy decisions 
and help avoid undue burdens for providers and access delays for patients. It is crucial for 
 
27 91 Fed. Reg. at 20013. 
13 
 
CMS to send a clear message to payers that in their step therapy decision-making, they 
should employ all clinical data to which they now have access rather than siloing utilization 
management from broader interoperability objectives.   
As the proposed rule notes, when a patient changes payers “the patient who previously 
failed a drug regimen may unexpectedly be subjected to new step therapy requirements, 
forcing them to switch from their current drug to whatever agent is the ‘first step’ in their new 
plan,” which can mean that “providers are unable to choose what they believe to be the best 
treatment options for their patients but instead must try alternative options first than have 
been mandated by the payer.”28  Where this outcome can be avoided through payers 
making better use of the data available to them through technology and payer-payer data-
sharing, it is imperative that this occur.  
We also urge CMS to consider modest guardrails around step therapy for payers subject to 
CMS regulation—and in CMS’ jawboning initiatives with additional payers.  Specifically, 
once a patient satisfies or obtains an exception to a step therapy protocol and receives 
coverage for the drug that is their prescriber’s first choice, the coverage should last for at 
least a year and should not lapse due to a change in dosage.  The burdens and risks of step 
therapy to providers and patients are substantial and well-documented.  Step therapy is the 
most extreme form of utilization management, and the effort involved in obtaining any type 
of prior authorization for a drug can be daunting – as CMS rightly notes,29 and as AMA’s 
recent survey illustrates.30  
This burden falls disproportionately on vulnerable patients, such as those with serious 
mental illness. Such patients’ medication regimens are often destabilized through prior 
authorization and reauthorization that leads to treatment abandonment and decreased 
adherence.   
Patients whose antipsychotic regimens were disrupted by payer-imposed requirements 
were nearly 12% more likely to discontinue all antipsychotic treatment compared with those 
without such disruptions. Patients with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder also had lower 
adherence after treatment disruptions.31 Requiring that patients undergo or seek exemption

from step therapy on a recurring basis needlessly disrupts care and impose unwarranted 
burdens on patients and providers alike.   
Therefore, once a patient satisfies or obtains an exception to a step therapy protocol, the 
patient should have the assurance of knowing that their prescriber’s first choice drug will be 
covered for a minimum period of at least one year and will remain covered for that period 
irrespective of whether any dosage adjustments may be needed. Providers should not be 
put in a position where making appropriate clinically based adjustments in a patient’s 
prescribed dosage for a drug could trigger a new round of step therapy and disrupt the 
continuity of their treatment. In addition, a dosage change alone should not require a new 
prior authorization. 
These are targeted reforms, which CMS could adopt on a near-term basis, that would 
improve access for many patients, especially those with serious or chronic diseases.  
Patients should have the assurance that once they have gone through step therapy and 
prior authorization, their regimen will be stable for a reasonable period and dosage 
adjustments will not upend their coverage. We hope CMS will consider initiating a future 
rulemaking process to adopt these guardrails.

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Lundbeck Pharmaceuticals LLC; signed by Devin Zatorski, Director, Federal and State Policy, Reimbursement and Strategy, Government Affairs.
- **Stakeholder type:** Other — biopharmaceutical manufacturer.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Global biopharmaceutical company focused on brain health, with more than 70 years in neuroscience; U.S. headquarters and facilities; 172 active U.S. clinical trial sites; R&D investment of 20-25% of global revenue.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Lundbeck strongly supports CMS efforts to extend electronic prior authorization reforms to drugs and emphasizes that the rule should maximize patient access, timeliness, and accountability. It asks CMS to adopt a uniform 24-hour drug prior authorization decision deadline across impacted payers, impose meaningful consequences for missed deadlines, standardize denial reasons, use PA metrics for oversight, and pursue near-term step therapy reforms.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; API-USAGE-METRICS; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS indirectly through electronic PA infrastructure; GENERAL/RFI on step therapy.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 91 Fed. Reg. 19890, 19933-19936, 19941, 19948-19949, 20013, 20039-20040; 42 CFR 422.568(b)(3), 422.568(f), 422.572(a)(2), 422.572(f); ACA section 1311(e)(1); Social Security Act sections 1852 and 1857.
- **Standards referenced:** Prior Authorization API, NCPDP standards, payer APIs, Payer-to-Payer API; no detailed discussion of specific FHIR IG versions.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Uniform 24-hour deadline for drug prior authorization**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Different deadlines across payer types create confusion and delay. Lundbeck argues that electronic PA functionality and payer access to requirements and documentation make a 24-hour deadline feasible and more aligned with patient access needs.
- **Specific request:** Require all impacted payers to respond to drug prior authorization requests within 24 hours.

**Topic 2: Accountability for missed PA deadlines**
- **Provision ID:** PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Deadlines without consequences may not change payer behavior and may still jeopardize timely access to medication.
- **Specific request:** Treat missed PA decision deadlines as automatic approvals; if CMS does not adopt that approach, treat missed deadlines as immediately appealable adverse determinations.

**Topic 3: Specific and actionable denial reasons**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Specific denial reasons help providers appeal, correct, resubmit, or choose alternatives; generic or unclear denials delay care.
- **Specific request:** Require standardized denial reason choices plus free-text fields for missing information, next steps, and actionable explanation; consider a standard denial reason form.

**Topic 4: Use PA metrics as an oversight tool**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Support with modifications
- **Rationale:** Granular metrics can help CMS detect unintended effects of shorter timelines, including increased denials, extensions, appeals, or overturned denials.
- **Specific request:** Monitor trends and outliers, require more granular reporting by drug group or therapeutic area, and publish synthesis reports for policymakers, researchers, patients, and other stakeholders.

**Topic 5: Step therapy reforms using payer data exchange**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Payer-to-payer data exchange can prevent patients from repeating step therapy after changing coverage and can identify contraindications or prior failures.
- **Specific request:** Require payers to use electronic tools and payer APIs to evaluate prior therapies; require step therapy approvals/exceptions to last at least one year and not lapse due to dosage changes.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S16:** Lundbeck supports requiring specific denial reasons and asks CMS to define specificity as actionable detail, using standardized reason categories and free text for next steps.
- **S17:** The comment supports structured standardized denial reasons, supplemented by narrative information where needed.
- **S20:** Lundbeck supports a 24-hour drug PA timeframe and urges CMS to apply it uniformly across all impacted payers.
- **S21:** The commenter states that a 24-hour timeframe is feasible because the proposed electronic PA tools and NCPDP standards support faster communication and decision-making.
- **S29:** Lundbeck supports metrics and requests more granular reporting, including drug groups, therapeutic areas, and brand/generic categories.
- **S34:** Lundbeck supports public reporting over time and recommends CMS use the data to publish synthesized reports and inform future rulemaking.
- **S35:** The comment supports public reporting and aggregate analysis but emphasizes that data should be granular enough to identify access problems.
- **S66-S82 / Step therapy RFI:** Lundbeck recommends requiring payers to use payer APIs and clinical history from other payers to evaluate step therapy and preserve continuity; it also recommends one-year stability for approvals and no new PA solely for dosage changes.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Require all impacted payers to respond to drug prior authorization requests within 24 hours.
2. Treat missed PA decision deadlines as deemed approvals, or at minimum immediately appealable denials.
3. Require standardized denial reasons with free-text fields for additional actionable details.
4. Use publicly reported PA metrics for CMS oversight of denials, extensions, appeals, and overturned decisions.
5. Require more granular PA metrics by drug group, therapeutic area, and generic/brand status.
6. Publish CMS synthesis reports based on PA metric trends and use findings in future rulemaking.
7. Require payers to use payer-to-payer data and APIs to determine whether step therapy requirements have already been satisfied.
8. Require step therapy approvals/exceptions to remain valid for at least one year and not lapse due to dosage changes.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Inconsistent payer deadlines; lack of accountability for missed deadlines; unclear denial explanations; insufficiently granular PA metrics; step therapy disruptions after payer changes or dosage changes.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Treatment delays, treatment abandonment, higher emergency department and inpatient use, missed doses, increased seizures, hospitalization, disrupted psychiatric medication regimens, reduced adherence, and increased provider burden.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Need for payer education, provider outreach, full use of electronic PA tools, and CMS oversight to avoid unintended increases in denials or extension requests.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Lundbeck cites migraine research finding one in five commercially insured patients experienced at least two payer denials due to PA/utilization management; pediatric epilepsy research reporting 38.4% encountered PA barriers, fewer than half received the originally prescribed medicine within seven days, with documented missed doses, increased seizures, and hospitalization; antipsychotic regimen disruption associated with nearly 12% higher likelihood of discontinuing all antipsychotic treatment.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Buse et al., Headache, January 2026; Wirell et al., Pediatric Neurology, June 2018; Fung et al., Medical Care, 2013; AMA/AJMC survey discussion; CMS Multi-Payer Alignment materials.
- **Examples provided:** Denials sometimes omit basic missing information such as an unsigned form or missing patient date of birth.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Patients needing medication, especially neurological, psychiatric, migraine, epilepsy, and serious mental illness populations; providers and staff; impacted payers; CMS and researchers.
- **Economic implications:** Potential reduction in health care utilization from faster medication access; lower provider administrative burden; need for payer investment in meeting deadlines and reporting.
- **Technical feasibility:** Commenter argues feasibility is improved by electronic PA tools, Prior Authorization API functions, NCPDP standards, and payer-to-payer data exchange.
- **Patient care impact:** Strongly positive if adopted; faster access, clearer next steps after denials, fewer treatment disruptions, and greater continuity during payer or dosage changes.

- **Overall position:** Supportive with modifications
- **Tone:** Professional, collaborative, patient-access focused
- **Priority level:** High
